overview:
usage: dataforge <command> [--flag value ...]

Commands, by phase:
  load:
    load                   Read a CSV file into a new frame Handle and report its shape.
  profile:
    describe-columns       Read full column profiles off a profile Handle, flagged columns first.
    describe-target        Read one declared target's problem type and statistics off a profile Handle.
    missingness            Read how missing values spread across rows, and which columns go missing together.
    profile                Profile a frame once into a profile Handle and return its Dataset Digest.
    top-associations       List the most strongly associated column pairs off a profile Handle, strongest first.
    value-summary          Read one column's top values, rare labels, bounds and percentiles off a profile Handle.
  split:
    split                  Split the frame behind a profile into a test frame and folds, each a new frame Handle.
  impute:
    compose-imputer        Compose a recipe's fitted units into an imputer Handle.
    explain-routing        Read the stored Routing Evidence behind each column's strategy.
    fit-unit               Train one unit of a recipe on a frame and return a unit Handle.
    impute                 Fill a frame with an imputer into a new frame Handle ready to model on.
    resolve-recipe         Resolve a routing into a recipe Handle that lists the units to fit.
    route                  Route every column of a profile to an imputation strategy, into a routing Handle.
  evaluate:
    c2st                   Test whether two frames come from the same distribution with a Classifier Two-Sample Test.
    describe-c2st-columns  Read columns' full C2ST results off a c2st Handle, flagged columns first.
    evaluate-imputation    Score how well an imputed frame keeps its data's distribution with a Classifier Two-Sample Test.
  workspace:
    export-frame           Write a frame Handle's data as a CSV file in the Workspace and return its path.
    list-handles           List the Workspace's Handles newest first, each with its Lineage and size.
    query-frame            Read raw cells, or measures of them per group, from any frame Handle: a loaded frame, a split fold or an imputed frame.

Go deeper:
  dataforge <command> --help    one command: flags, result, errors, an example
  dataforge schema <command> <argument> [path]
                                one nested argument's schema, one level at a time
  The `dataforge` Skill (SKILL.md) teaches the workflow and what each exit code asks.
  dataforge install --skills [--global]
                                install the Skill for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor

Every command prints one JSON value on stdout, errors too. Exit codes: 0 success,
2 InvalidInput, 3 UnknownName, 4 Conflict, 5 Infeasible, 6 IncompatibleArtifact,
1 Unexpected. A list of records prints as {"fields": [...], "rows": [[...], ...]}.

Workspace Settings, set by the Operator; leave them as they are:
  --workspace, --literal-policy, --declared-inputs, --core-budget
--progress prints one line per Pipeline Event to stderr.

commands.c2st:
usage: dataforge c2st --reference <string> --candidate <string> [--repeats <integer>] [--scheme <scheme>] [--seed <integer>] [--thresholds <json>]

Test whether two frames come from the same distribution with a Classifier Two-Sample Test.

Use when:
  Call this to check drift between two frames, such as a `split` fold's `train` frame
  and the `test` frame. A classifier learns to tell `reference` rows from `candidate`
  rows; if it does no better than chance on held-out rows, the frames are
  indistinguishable. Each repeat subsamples the larger frame to the smaller one's size.
  Columns either frame declares excluded or soft-excluded are left out; every other
  column must be in both frames. String columns cannot be tested: exclude them on
  `profile` before `split`. No Handle is written.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --reference <string>, required
      A frame Handle, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`: the baseline, such as the training rows.
  --candidate <string>, required
      A frame Handle to compare against `reference`, such as the test rows.
  --repeats <integer>, optional
      Balanced subsampling repeats, from 1 to 100. More repeats steady `mean_repeat_z`.
      Null means 5. Constraints: at least 1; at most 100.
  --scheme <one of split|cross_validation>, optional
      `split` fits once per repeat on a 70/30 carve; `cross_validation` fits five times
      per repeat and scores every drawn row, at five times the cost. Null means `split`.
  --seed <integer>, optional
      Seed of the subsampling, the carve and the classifier. Null means a fixed default,
      so the same call gives the same result. Constraints: at least 0; at most
      4294967295.
  --thresholds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      The size floor and the classifier's leaf size, each with its default and range.
      Fields: dataforge schema c2st thresholds

Returns C2STRun, as one JSON object:
  reference: string
      The reference frame Handle read.
  candidate: string
      The candidate frame Handle read.
  reference_rows: integer
      Rows of `reference`.
  candidate_rows: integer
      Rows of `candidate`. Each repeat draws the smaller frame's row count from each.
  columns: integer
      Columns tested: those of `reference` that neither frame declares excluded or soft-
      excluded.
  skipped: integer
      Columns of `reference` left out because a frame declares them excluded or soft-
      excluded.
  scheme: one of split|cross_validation
      The scheme used.
  repeats: integer
      The repeats run.
  seed: integer
      The seed used: yours, or the fixed default when you passed null.
  mean_repeat_z: number
      The headline: the mean of `repeat_z`. Near 0 means the classifier could not tell
      the frames apart; about 2 or more means it could, so the frames differ.
  repeat_z: list of number
      One `z` per repeat, in repeat order: `(accuracy - 0.5) * 2 * sqrt(n_test)`.
  repeat_z_spread: number
      Standard deviation of `repeat_z`; 0 for one repeat. Large next to `mean_repeat_z`
      means the mean rests on lucky draws: raise `repeats`.
  train_accuracy: number
      Mean training accuracy over the repeats. Near 1 beside a `test_accuracy` near 0.5
      means the classifier memorised rows, which hides a difference rather than
      inventing one.
  test_accuracy: number
      Mean held-out accuracy over the repeats; 0.5 is chance.
  n_test: integer
      Held-out rows scored in each repeat, half from each frame.
  degenerate: true|false
      True when every repeat's classifier predicted one frame for every row, so `z` says
      nothing. Compare larger frames, or lower `thresholds.min_samples_leaf`.
  unseen_category: true|false
      True when a categorical or boolean value is in `candidate` and never in
      `reference`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `reference` or `candidate` names no frame Handle in this Workspace. `candidates`
      lists frame Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `reference` or `candidate` is a Handle of another kind.
  frames_not_aligned (2)
      A column to test is in only one frame. `columns` names them.
  c2st_string_column (5)
      A column to test is a string column. `columns` names them.
  c2st_sample_floor (5)
      The smaller frame has fewer rows than `thresholds.min_rows`.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range, or every column is
      excluded.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `reference` or `candidate`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  impute: Fill a frame before comparing it.
  profile: Exclude string columns, which the frames `split` makes inherit.
  split: Make the train, validation and test frames to compare.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e --exclude-columns city
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge split --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --scheme '{"kind":"random","test_size":0.5}'
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...,"test":"frame_2c3d4e5f",...,"rows":[[0,0,"frame_3d4e5f6a",...]]},...}
  $ dataforge c2st --reference frame_3d4e5f6a --candidate frame_2c3d4e5f --thresholds '{"min_rows":3}'
  {...,"reference":"frame_3d4e5f6a","candidate":"frame_2c3d4e5f",...,"columns":2,"skipped":1,...}
commands.compose-imputer:
usage: dataforge compose-imputer --recipe <string> --units <array>

Compose a recipe's fitted units into an imputer Handle.

Use when:
  Call this after `fit_unit` has trained every unit `resolve_recipe` listed, to get one
  imputer that fills the whole frame. Pass one unit Handle per unit, in any order. Every
  unit must have been fitted from this recipe, and every unit of the recipe needs one
  Handle; columns routed to `passthrough`, `dropped` or `indicator` have no unit and
  need none. The imputer Handle names the recipe and its unit Handles and holds nothing
  else, so the call is quick and copies no fitted model. To change one unit, fit it
  again with `fit_unit`, such as on another frame or seed, and compose again with the
  new unit Handle in place of the old one: that writes only a new imputer Handle, and
  the old imputer stays as it was. To change hyperparameters or estimates, resolve a new
  recipe and fit its units, since units of another recipe are refused.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --recipe <string>, required
      A recipe Handle, such as `recipe_7f3a9c2e`.
  --units <list of string>, required
      Unit Handles, one per unit of the recipe, such as `["unit_3c4d5e6f",
      "unit_9a8b7c6d"]`. Empty when the recipe has no unit.

Returns ComposeImputerResult, as one JSON object:
  imputer: string
      Imputer Handle, such as `imputer_7f3a9c2e`. It names the recipe and the unit
      Handles, and holds nothing else.
  recipe: string
      The recipe Handle read.
  units: table of (unit_id, strategy, unit)
      Every unit of the recipe, in routing order, with the unit Handle composed for it.
      Empty when no column fills values. At most 50; past 50, `omitted` counts the rest.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `recipe` or a `units` entry names no Handle of its kind in this Workspace.
      `candidates` lists Handles of that kind, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `recipe` or a `units` entry is a Handle of another kind.
  unit_recipe_mismatch (4)
      Units were fitted from another recipe. `params` names them, such as `units[2]`.
  duplicate_key (2)
      Two unit Handles fill the same unit. `params` names every one after the first.
  unit_coverage_mismatch (2)
      A unit of the recipe has no unit Handle. The message names the units; `columns`
      names the columns they fill.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `recipe` or a unit.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  fit-unit: Make the unit Handles to compose.
  list-handles: Find unit and imputer Handles made earlier.
  resolve-recipe: List the units a recipe needs.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
  $ dataforge fit-unit --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --unit-id median:income
  {...,"unit":"unit_3c4d5e6f",...}
  $ dataforge compose-imputer --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --units unit_3c4d5e6f
  {...,"imputer":"imputer_4d5e6f7a","recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
commands.describe-c2st-columns:
usage: dataforge describe-c2st-columns --report <string> [--names <array>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

Read columns' full C2ST results off a c2st Handle, flagged columns first.

Use when:
  Call this after `evaluate_imputation` to dig into a column's score: each frame's `z`
  per repeat, its accuracies, and the provenance (the classifier, its parameters and the
  settings the run used). It reads the stored report only, so it is cheap and never
  recomputes. Filter with `names`, then page with `offset` and `limit`. The same
  arguments always return the same page.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --report <string>, required
      A c2st Handle `evaluate_imputation` made, such as `c2st_6a7b8c9d`.
  --names <list of string>, optional
      Only these columns. Null means every evaluated column.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many matching columns to skip, for the next page. Null means 0. Constraints:
      at least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most columns to return, from 1 to 20. Null means 20. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 20.

Returns DescribeC2STColumnsResult, as one JSON object:
  report: string
      The c2st Handle read.
  total: integer
      How many columns match `names`.
  offset: integer
      How many matching columns this page skipped.
  columns: table of (column, outcome, verdict, annotations, n_observed, n_filled, score)
      Matching columns: `flagged` ones first, then dataset order. At most 20; when more
      remain, `omitted` counts them and names `describe_c2st_columns`.
  provenance: object
      The classifier, its parameters, the scikit-learn version and the settings of the
      run.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `report` names no c2st Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists c2st Handles,
      newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `report` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      A name in `names` was not evaluated: it is not a column, or it was excluded or
      `dropped`. `candidates` lists close matches; `issues` lists every unknown name.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `report`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  evaluate-imputation: Make the c2st Handle and its outcome census.
  route: Route a flagged column to another strategy.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
  $ dataforge fit-unit --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --unit-id median:income
  {...,"unit":"unit_3c4d5e6f",...}
  $ dataforge compose-imputer --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --units unit_3c4d5e6f
  {...,"imputer":"imputer_4d5e6f7a",...}
  $ dataforge impute --imputer imputer_4d5e6f7a --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"frame":"frame_8b9c0d1e",...}
  $ dataforge evaluate-imputation --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --imputed frame_8b9c0d1e
  {...,"c2st":"c2st_6a7b8c9d",...}
  $ dataforge describe-c2st-columns --report c2st_6a7b8c9d --names income
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"report":"c2st_6a7b8c9d","total":1,"offset":0,...}
commands.describe-columns:
usage: dataforge describe-columns --profile <string> [--names <array>] [--flagged-only <boolean>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

Read full column profiles off a profile Handle, flagged columns first.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` to read more about columns than the Dataset Digest shows:
  every statistic for the column's semantic type, the missing-value counts, the flags
  and how the type was decided. It reads the stored profile only, so it is cheap and
  never recomputes. It holds no cell values; for top values, bounds and percentiles call
  `value_summary`. Filter with `names` or `flagged_only`, then page with `offset` and
  `limit`. The same arguments always return the same page.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`.
  --names <list of string>, optional
      Only these columns. Null means every profiled and skipped column.
  --flagged-only <true|false>, optional
      True keeps only columns that raised a flag. Null means false.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many matching columns to skip, for the next page. Null means 0. Constraints:
      at least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most columns to return, from 1 to 15. Null means 15. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 15.

Returns DescribeColumnsResult, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      The profile Handle read.
  total: integer
      How many columns match the filters.
  offset: integer
      How many matching columns this page skipped.
  columns: table of (column, role, semantic_type, numeric_kind, dtype, parsed_dtype, type_flags, flags, cardinality, missingness, stats)
      Matching columns: flagged ones first, then dataset order. At most 15; when more
      remain, `omitted` counts them and names `describe_columns`.
  flag_dials: table of (flag, dials)
      One entry per flag raised on a column of this page, in `columns` order of first
      appearance.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` names no profile Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists profile
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      A name in `names` is not a column of the profile. `candidates` lists close
      matches; `issues` lists every unknown name.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  missingness: Read every co-missing pair.
  profile: Make the profile Handle and its Dataset Digest.
  value-summary: Read one column's top values, bounds and percentiles.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge describe-columns --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --names age,city
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","total":2,"offset":0,...}
commands.describe-target:
usage: dataforge describe-target --profile <string> --name <string>

Read one declared target's problem type and statistics off a profile Handle.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` with `targets` set, to see what kind of learning problem a
  target poses and what to watch for: missing target values, class imbalance or a skewed
  numeric target. A classification target lists its most common classes with their
  labels; a regression target gives its distribution. Class labels are cell values, so
  they are Literal Fields. To rank features against the target, call `top_associations`
  with `column` set to it. It reads the stored profile only, so it is cheap and never
  recomputes.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`.
  --name <string>, required
      A target declared when the profile was made.

Returns DescribeTargetResult, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      The profile Handle read.
  column: string
      The target column.
  problem_type: one of regression|binary_classification|multiclass_classification|unknown
      The learning problem the target implies.
  missing_count: integer
      Rows whose target is missing.
  missing_ratio: number
      Share of rows whose target is missing.
  flags: list of one of contains_missing|high_imbalance|severe_imbalance|highly_skewed|is_identifier
      Problems with the target: `contains_missing`, `high_imbalance` (dominant class
      ratio above 5), `severe_imbalance` (above 20), `highly_skewed` or `is_identifier`.
  distribution: object
      Statistics of a numeric target, as `describe_columns` gives them; null for a
      classification target.
  classes: object
      Classes of a classification target; null for a regression target.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` names no profile Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists profile
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      `name` is not a target declared on the profile. `candidates` lists the declared
      targets closest to it.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  profile: Declare targets and make the profile Handle.
  top-associations: Rank features against the target.
  value-summary: Read every class label, or a target's bounds and percentiles.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e --targets income
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge describe-target --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --name income
  {...,"column":"income","problem_type":"regression","missing_count":1,...}
commands.evaluate-imputation:
usage: dataforge evaluate-imputation --profile <string> --imputed <string> [--seed <integer>] [--thresholds <json>]

Score how well an imputed frame keeps its data's distribution with a Classifier Two-Sample Test.

Use when:
  Call this after `impute` to check the fill. For each column, a classifier learns to
  tell the rows where the column was filled from the rows where it was observed, reading
  whole rows of `imputed`; if it does no better than chance, the fill is
  indistinguishable from real data. `imputed` is scored against the frame it was filled
  from, so pass the profile the imputer was routed on, even for a filled fold. Columns
  either Handle excludes and `dropped` columns are not evaluated. Read `census` first,
  then the `flagged` columns. A column filled with one value (`mean`, `median`, `mode`
  or `constant`) is expected to be flagged: judge a model-based column against those.
  Under missing at random, the observed and filled rows are meant to differ, so a flag
  cannot tell a bad fill from strongly MAR missingness: the `z` is true, but it may not
  be the imputation's fault. The result writes a `c2st_` Handle holding every column's
  per-frame results and the provenance.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`: the one the imputer was routed on.
      Its sentinels and semantic types decide which cells were filled and which columns
      can be tested.
  --imputed <string>, required
      A frame Handle `impute` made, such as `frame_5b6c7d8e`.
  --seed <integer>, optional
      Seed of the subsampling, the carve and the classifier. Null means a fixed default,
      so the same call gives the same result. Constraints: at least 0; at most
      4294967295.
  --thresholds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      The size floor, the classifier's leaf size, the annotation bands and the false
      discovery rate, each with its default and range.
      Fields: dataforge schema evaluate-imputation thresholds

Returns EvaluateImputationResult, as one JSON object:
  c2st: string
      The new C2ST report Handle, such as `c2st_7f3a9c2e`. It holds every column's per-
      frame results and the provenance.
  profile: string
      The profile Handle read.
  imputed: string
      The imputed frame Handle read.
  source_frame: string
      The frame Handle `imputed` was filled from: the observed values it is scored
      against.
  rows: integer
      Rows of `imputed`.
  seed: integer
      The seed used: yours, or the fixed default when you passed null.
  census: table of (outcome, verdict, count)
      Columns per outcome and verdict, over every evaluated column. Read it first.
  columns: table of (column, outcome, verdict, mean_frame_z, p_adjusted, annotations, n_observed, n_filled)
      Every evaluated column: `flagged` ones first, then dataset order. Excluded and
      `dropped` columns are not evaluated. At most 100; past 100, `omitted` counts the
      rest and names `describe_c2st_columns`.
  outcome_dials: table of (outcome, dials)
      One entry per threshold-decided outcome, verdict or annotation any evaluated
      column has, with the dials that decide it.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` or `imputed` names no Handle of its kind in this Workspace. `candidates`
      lists Handles of that kind, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` or `imputed` is a Handle of another kind.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range, or `imputed` was not made
      by `impute`.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`, `imputed` or the frame it was
      filled from.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  c2st: Compare two frames, such as a fold's train and test frames.
  impute: Make the imputed frame to score.
  route: Route a flagged column to another strategy.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
  $ dataforge fit-unit --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --unit-id median:income
  {...,"unit":"unit_3c4d5e6f",...}
  $ dataforge compose-imputer --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --units unit_3c4d5e6f
  {...,"imputer":"imputer_4d5e6f7a",...}
  $ dataforge impute --imputer imputer_4d5e6f7a --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"frame":"frame_8b9c0d1e",...}
  $ dataforge evaluate-imputation --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --imputed frame_8b9c0d1e
  {...,"c2st":"c2st_6a7b8c9d","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","imputed":"frame_8b9c0d1e",...}
commands.explain-routing:
usage: dataforge explain-routing --routing <string> [--columns <array>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

Read the stored Routing Evidence behind each column's strategy.

Use when:
  Call this after `route` to see how close a column came to another strategy. Its
  Routing Evidence is the facts behind its Routing Reason: why it reached the Signal
  Score check, the Signal Score (how well other columns predict it, from 0 to 1) and its
  parts, the Signal Tier the score fell in (which picks a model or a plain fill), and
  each Feasibility check (whether the data can train `mice` or `knn`) with its failed
  terms and the dial that would change them. For each column's strategy and reason
  alone, `route`'s own result already has them; do not call this. It reads only what the
  routing Handle stores, so it works on a routing made in another process or by another
  Agent, and never recomputes. A column you declared in `strategies` has empty evidence,
  except one `feasibility` check when its strategy is `knn`, `mice`,
  `cluster_conditional` or `gmm_sampling`. Filter with `columns`, then page with
  `offset` and `limit`. The same arguments always return the same page.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --routing <string>, required
      A routing Handle, such as `routing_7f3a9c2e`.
  --columns <list of string>, optional
      Only these columns. Null means every routed column.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many matching columns to skip, for the next page. Null means 0. Constraints:
      at least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most columns to return, from 1 to 15. Null means 15. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 15.

Returns ExplainRoutingResult, as one JSON object:
  routing: string
      The routing Handle read.
  profile: string
      The profile Handle the routing was made from.
  total: integer
      How many columns match `columns`.
  offset: integer
      How many matching columns this page skipped.
  columns: table of (column, strategy, reason, entry, signal_score, tier, feasibility)
      Matching columns in `route`'s order: those that fill or drop first, then
      `passthrough`. At most 15; when more remain, `omitted` counts them and names
      `explain_routing`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `routing` names no routing Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists routing
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `routing` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      A name in `columns` is not a routed column; excluded columns are not routed.
      `candidates` lists close matches; `issues` lists every unknown name.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `routing`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find routing Handles made earlier.
  route: Make the routing Handle and each column's Routing Reason.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge explain-routing --routing routing_5a6b7c8d --columns income
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","total":1,"offset":0,...}
commands.export-frame:
usage: dataforge export-frame --frame <string>

Write a frame Handle's data as a CSV file in the Workspace and return its path.

Use when:
  Call this to hand a frame on as a file: a split fold, an imputed frame, or a loaded
  one. The file goes into the Workspace's `exports/` folder, named after the Handle; you
  cannot choose where it goes. Exporting the same Handle again returns the same path and
  writes nothing, because a frame never changes. A CSV keeps no dtypes, so reading it
  back may infer types again. Exporting never changes the Handle: to change the data,
  change the declarations and call the Operation that made it again.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --frame <string>, required
      A frame Handle, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`.

Returns ExportFrameResult, as one JSON object:
  path: string
      Absolute path of the CSV, inside the Workspace's `exports/` folder.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `frame` names no frame Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists up to 5 frame
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `frame` is a Handle of another kind. `allowed` names `frame`.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `frame`. Load it again.
  invalid_argument (2)
      `frame` is missing or not a string.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find a frame Handle to export.
  load: Make a frame Handle from a CSV file.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge export-frame --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"path":".../exports/frame_7f3a9c2e.csv"}
commands.fit-unit:
usage: dataforge fit-unit --recipe <string> --unit-id <string> [--frame <string>] [--seed <integer>]

Train one unit of a recipe on a frame and return a unit Handle.

Use when:
  Call this after `resolve_recipe`, once per unit it lists, to train the imputer piece
  by piece. There is no call that trains them all: you fit each unit yourself, in any
  order, and can run them side by side. The unit trains on the frame the recipe's
  profile was made from, or on `frame` when you pass one, such as a `split` fold, with
  the hyperparameters and estimates the recipe holds. The result is a unit Handle and
  the fit's signals: the estimator that ran, whether an iterative model converged, how
  many iterations it ran, and the dials it trained with. Read `warnings` first: a model
  that hit its iteration cap fits, but comes back with a coded warning saying which dial
  to turn. To change how a unit trains, call `resolve_recipe` again with new
  hyperparameters or estimates and fit that recipe's unit. `seed` fixes the random
  draws, such as those `gmm_sampling` fills with; null uses a fixed default, so the same
  call gives the same unit twice.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --recipe <string>, required
      A recipe Handle, such as `recipe_7f3a9c2e`.
  --unit-id <string>, required
      The unit to train, as `resolve_recipe` lists it: `mice` or `knn` for a joint
      block, `<strategy>:<column>` for one column, such as `median:age`.
  --frame <string>, optional
      A frame Handle to train on, such as a `split` fold. It must have every column of
      the recipe's routing. Null uses the frame the recipe's profile was made from.
  --seed <integer>, optional
      Seed of the random draws, from 0 to 4294967295. Null uses the fixed default.
      Constraints: at least 0; at most 4294967295.

Returns FitUnitResult, as one JSON object:
  unit: string
      Fitted unit Handle, such as `unit_7f3a9c2e`.
  recipe: string
      The recipe Handle read.
  frame: string
      The frame Handle the unit trained on: yours, or the frame the recipe's profile was
      made from.
  unit_id: string
      The unit trained, as `resolve_recipe` lists it.
  strategy: one of mean|median|mode|knn|mice|mnar|constant|cluster_conditional|gmm_sampling
      The strategy the unit trained.
  columns: list of string
      The columns the unit fills, in dataset order. At most 100; past 100, `omitted`
      counts the rest and names `explain_routing`.
  seed: integer
      The seed used: yours, or the fixed default when you passed null.
  signals: object
      What the fit did. Caveats on it, such as a model that hit its iteration cap, are
      in `warnings`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `recipe` or `frame` names no Handle of its kind in this Workspace. `candidates`
      lists Handles of that kind, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `recipe` or `frame` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_unit (3)
      The recipe has no unit `unit_id`. `candidates` lists close matches.
  missing_fitted_columns (2)
      `frame` lacks columns of the recipe's routing. `columns` names them.
  unit_not_trainable (5)
      The unit cannot train on the frame, such as a bimodal column with no mode centres
      or a column with too few values. `columns` names its columns; the message gives
      the reason.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type, or `seed` is out of range.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `recipe` or the frame.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find unit Handles made earlier.
  resolve-recipe: Make the recipe Handle and list its unit ids.
  split: Make folds to train on.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
  $ dataforge fit-unit --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --unit-id median:income
  {...,"unit":"unit_3c4d5e6f","recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b","frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e","unit_id":"median:income","strategy":"median",...}
commands.impute:
usage: dataforge impute --imputer <string> --frame <string>

Fill a frame with an imputer into a new frame Handle ready to model on.

Use when:
  Call this after `compose_imputer`, once per frame to fill: the frame the units were
  fitted on, a `split` fold or the test frame. The imputer applies what it learned and
  learns nothing from `frame`, so filling a test frame leaks nothing. The new frame
  leaves out hard-excluded columns and the `dropped` columns you declared, and has every
  indicator column; the source frame keeps them. A Drop Candidate, a column routing
  marked `dropped` for its missing share, stays in the new frame with its missing
  values: `drop_candidates` lists them and the dial that flagged them, and dropping one
  is your call. An `mnar` column keeps its nulls beside its `<column>_missing`
  indicator: its fill is on record in `columns` and is not applied. `passthrough`
  columns keep their missing values too. `frame` must have every column the imputer
  fills or leaves as it is, and no column it was not fitted on, other than excluded
  ones. The new frame inherits the source frame's declarations and the exclusions the
  routing added, and declares each indicator column a Soft Exclusion: later phases keep
  it but skip it.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --imputer <string>, required
      An imputer Handle, such as `imputer_7f3a9c2e`.
  --frame <string>, required
      A frame Handle to fill, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`.

Returns ImputeResult, as one JSON object:
  frame: string
      The new frame Handle, such as `frame_5b6c7d8e`. It lacks hard-excluded and
      `dropped` columns other than Drop Candidates, has the indicator columns as Soft
      Exclusions later phases skip, and inherits the source frame's declarations.
  imputer: string
      The imputer Handle read.
  source_frame: string
      The frame Handle filled. It stays as it was, excluded columns included.
  rows: integer
      Rows of the new frame: as many as the source frame.
  columns: table of (column, strategy, missing, filled, fill_value)
      Every column the imputer was fitted on: those that fill or drop first, then
      `passthrough`, each group in dataset order. At most 100; past 100, `omitted`
      counts the rest.
  drop_candidates: object
      Columns the library would drop, kept in the new frame: every drop is the Agent's
      own. To drop them, pass them to `route` as `exclude_columns` and build the imputer
      again from there. Null when there are none.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `imputer` or `frame` names no Handle of its kind in this Workspace. `candidates`
      lists Handles of that kind, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `imputer` or `frame` is a Handle of another kind.
  unseen_column (2)
      `frame` has columns the imputer was not fitted on and no declaration excludes.
      `columns` names them.
  missing_fitted_columns (2)
      `frame` lacks columns the imputer fills or leaves as it is. `columns` names them.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `imputer`, a Handle it names, or `frame`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  compose-imputer: Make the imputer Handle.
  export-frame: Write the new frame as a CSV file.
  split: Make folds and a test frame to fill.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b",...}
  $ dataforge fit-unit --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --unit-id median:income
  {...,"unit":"unit_3c4d5e6f",...}
  $ dataforge compose-imputer --recipe recipe_9e0f1a2b --units unit_3c4d5e6f
  {...,"imputer":"imputer_4d5e6f7a",...}
  $ dataforge impute --imputer imputer_4d5e6f7a --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"frame":"frame_8b9c0d1e","imputer":"imputer_4d5e6f7a","source_frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e","rows":6,...}
commands.list-handles:
usage: dataforge list-handles [--kind <kind>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

List the Workspace's Handles newest first, each with its Lineage and size.

Use when:
  Call this to find Handles made earlier: after a restart, as a sub-agent sharing the
  Workspace, or when you have lost track of a Handle string. Each Handle comes with its
  Lineage, which is the Operation that made it, the arguments it was passed, and the
  Handles it read. Read the Lineage to tell two Handles of the same kind apart. Handles
  never expire and are never deleted, so an old Handle stays usable. This reads only
  stored records, never dataset rows.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --kind <one of frame|profile|routing|recipe|unit|imputer|c2st>, optional
      Only Handles of this kind: `frame`, `profile`, `routing`, `recipe`, `unit`,
      `imputer` or `c2st`. Null lists every kind.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many of the newest Handles to skip, for the next page. Null means 0.
      Constraints: at least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most Handles to return, from 1 to 12. Null means 12. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 12.

Returns ListHandlesResult, as one JSON object:
  total: integer
      How many Handles of the asked kind exist in the Workspace.
  offset: integer
      How many of the newest Handles this page skipped.
  handles: table of (handle, kind, operation, arguments, inputs, size)
      Handles, newest first. At most 12; when more remain, `omitted` counts them and
      names `list_handles`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  invalid_argument (2)
      `kind` is not a Handle kind, or `offset` or `limit` is out of range.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  export-frame: Write a frame Handle out as CSV.
  load: Make a frame Handle from a CSV file.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge list-handles --kind frame
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"total":1,"offset":0,
  "handles":{"fields":["handle","kind","operation","arguments","inputs","size"],
  "rows":[["frame_7f3a9c2e","frame","load",
  {"fields":["name","value","value_cut"],"rows":[["path","\"train.csv\"",false]]},
  [],{"fields":["measure","value"],"rows":[["rows",6],["columns",3]]}]]}}
commands.load:
usage: dataforge load --path <string>

Read a CSV file into a new frame Handle and report its shape.

Use when:
  Call this first, once per dataset. If the Operator declared inputs, only those paths
  load, and any other path is refused, including an edited copy of a declared file. With
  none declared, any CSV path loads. Every later Operation reads the data through the
  returned frame Handle: a short string such as `frame_7f3a9c2e` naming the stored
  frame, which never changes. Loading the same path twice makes two Handles over
  identical data.

  --path <string>, required
      Path of the CSV file, exactly as you were given it. A relative path is resolved
      from the working directory.

  frame: string
      Frame Handle for the loaded data, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`.
  n_rows: integer
      Number of data rows, not counting the header.
  n_columns: integer
      Number of columns, including any not listed in `columns`.
  columns: table of (column, dtype)
      Columns in CSV header order, at most 100. Past 100, `omitted` counts the rest.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  input_not_declared (2)
      The Operator declared inputs and `path` is not one of them. Nothing is loaded or

  input_not_found (2)

      The file could not be read as CSV. Stop and report it.

See Also:
  export-frame: Write a frame Handle out as CSV.
  list-handles: Find frame Handles made earlier in this Workspace.

commands.missingness:
usage: dataforge missingness --profile <string> [--column <string>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

Read how missing values spread across rows, and which columns go missing together.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` when columns have missing values, to decide whether to drop
  rows and whether values are missing at random. It gives how many values each row is
  missing, and the column pairs whose missing values fall on the same rows, most co-
  missing first. Columns that go missing together suggest the values are missing for a
  reason, which matters for imputation. It reads the stored profile only, so it is cheap
  and never recomputes. The same arguments always return the same page.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`.
  --column <string>, optional
      Only pairs that include this column, which is then always `column_a`. Null means
      every pair.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many matching pairs to skip, for the next page. Null means 0. Constraints: at
      least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most pairs to return, from 1 to 100. Null means 100. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 100.

Returns MissingnessResult, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      The profile Handle read.
  sparsity: number
      Share of all cells that are missing.
  columns_with_missing: integer
      Profiled columns missing at least one value.
  rows: object
      How many values each row is missing.
  total: integer
      How many pairs match the filter. Only columns missing at least one value form
      pairs.
  offset: integer
      How many matching pairs this page skipped.
  pairs: table of (column_a, column_b, correlation, mar_suspect)
      Matching pairs, most co-missing (highest `correlation`) first, ties in dataset
      order. At most 100; when more remain, `omitted` counts them and names
      `missingness`.
  mar_suspect_dial: object
      The `profile` dial behind `mar_suspect`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` names no profile Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists profile
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      `column` is not a column of the profile. `candidates` lists close matches.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  describe-columns: Read each column's missing-value counts.
  profile: Make the profile Handle and its Dataset Digest.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge missingness --profile profile_1b2c3d4e
  {"warnings":...,"omitted":...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...,"columns_with_missing":2,...}
commands.profile:
usage: dataforge profile --frame <string> [--semantic-types <json>] [--numeric-kinds <json>] [--sentinels <json>] [--datetime-formats <json>] [--targets <array>] [--exclude-columns <array>] [--skip-columns <array>] [--seed <integer>] [--thresholds <json>]

Profile a frame once into a profile Handle and return its Dataset Digest.

Use when:
  Call this once per frame, right after `load`. It computes every column statistic,
  association and nonlinearity probe once and stores them in a profile Handle, which
  carries its frame. Every later step reads the profile, never the raw data. The Dataset
  Digest is the dataset at low resolution: row and column counts, duplicates, sparsity,
  targets, your declarations, and one row per column with flagged columns first. It
  holds no cell values. Declarations made here, and those the frame inherited, are
  recorded on the profile and passed down to every frame made from it. To change a
  declaration or a dial, call `profile` again; that makes a new profile Handle and
  leaves the old one as it was.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --frame <string>, required
      A frame Handle, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`.
  --semantic-types <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Semantic types you set instead of detection, one entry per column.
      Fields: dataforge schema profile semantic_types
  --numeric-kinds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Numeric kinds you set instead of detection, one entry per numeric column.
      Fields: dataforge schema profile numeric_kinds
  --sentinels <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Values that mean "missing" in a column, one entry per column.
      Fields: dataforge schema profile sentinels
  --datetime-formats <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      How to read datetime columns, one entry per column.
      Fields: dataforge schema profile datetime_formats
  --targets <list of string>, optional
      Target columns. Null means none.
  --exclude-columns <list of string>, optional
      Columns to leave out of this and every later phase, added to what the frame
      already excludes. Null means none.
  --skip-columns <list of string>, optional
      Columns profiling skips but later phases still see. Null means none.
  --seed <integer>, optional
      Seed for every random step: mixture fits, mutual information and the nonlinearity
      probes. Null means a fixed default, so the same call gives the same result.
      Constraints: at least 0; at most 4294967295.
  --thresholds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Dials, grouped by what they judge, each with its default and range.
      Fields: dataforge schema profile thresholds

Returns ProfileResult, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      Profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`. It carries its frame and these
      declarations.
  frame: string
      The frame Handle that was profiled.
  n_rows: integer
      Number of rows.
  n_columns: integer
      Number of columns in the frame, excluded ones included.
  duplicate_rows: integer
      Number of rows that repeat an earlier row exactly.
  duplicate_ratio: number
      Share of rows that repeat an earlier row.
  sparsity: number
      Share of all cells that are missing.
  targets: table of (column, problem_type, missing_ratio)
      Declared targets and their problem types.
  declarations: object
      Your declarations as recorded on the profile.
  columns: table of (column, role, semantic_type, numeric_kind, null_ratio, severity, cardinality, skew, outlier_density, flags)
      Profiled and skipped columns: flagged ones first, then dataset order. At most 100;
      past 100, `omitted` counts the rest and names `describe_columns`.
  flag_dials: table of (flag, dials)
      One entry per flag raised on any column, in `columns` order of first appearance.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `frame` names no frame Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists frame Handles,
      newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `frame` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      A declaration names a column the frame lacks. `candidates` lists close matches;
      `issues` lists every problem argument.
  duplicate_key (2)
      A declaration list names the same column twice.
  declaration_conflict (4)
      Two declarations contradict: a numeric kind on a column declared non-numeric, a
      target that is excluded or skipped, or a declaration that differs from one the
      frame inherited.
  invalid_dial_value (2)
      Two dials are out of order, such as `severity_minor` above `severity_moderate`.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range.
  override_coercion_failed (5)
      No value of a column converts to its declared type.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `frame`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find profile Handles made earlier.
  load: Make the frame Handle to profile.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e --targets income
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e","n_rows":6,"n_columns":3,...}
commands.query-frame:
usage: dataforge query-frame --frame <string> [--filter <json>] [--mode <json>]

Read raw cells, or measures of them per group, from any frame Handle: a loaded frame, a split fold or an imputed frame.

Use when:
  Call this to look at actual rows: to check that a sentinel such as `-999` is where you
  think, to see what an imputation filled, or to eyeball a fold. Cells come back exactly
  as stored. Declared sentinels are not read as missing, so `-999` shows as `-999`;
  `missingness` gives the profile's view of what is missing. `filter` keeps the rows
  that pass any one of its AND-lists, such as every row where `amount` is `-999`. Rows
  mode returns up to `limit` matching rows, each with its position in the frame: the
  first ones in dataset order, a seeded `random` sample, or the extremes of one column
  in `sort` order. Aggregate mode summarises the matching rows instead: counts and
  statistics per group of up to 3 key columns, such as the mean `income` per `city`. The
  cells, group keys, `min`, `max` and `median` are in Literal Fields. It never makes a
  Handle and never changes the frame.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --frame <string>, required
      A frame Handle, such as `frame_7f3a9c2e`.
  --filter <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      An OR of up to 5 AND-lists, each of 1 to 10 `{"column": ..., "op": ..., "value":
      ...}` predicates.
      Fields: dataforge schema query-frame filter
  --mode <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Rows mode is `{"kind": "rows", "columns": [...], "limit": n, "order": {...}}`.
      Fields: dataforge schema query-frame mode

Returns QueryFrameResult, as one JSON object:
  frame: string
      The frame Handle read.
  mode: one of rows|aggregate
      The mode that ran.
  total_rows: integer
      Rows in the frame.
  matched_rows: integer
      Rows that match the filter, counted exactly over every row, past any cap. With no
      filter, every row matches.
  row_positions: list of integer
      Rows mode: each returned row's position in the frame, from 0, in returned order.
      When more rows match, `omitted` counts them. Null in aggregate mode.
  group_count: integer
      Aggregate mode: how many groups the matching rows form, counted exactly, past the
      cap of 100. Null in rows mode.
  group_sizes: list of integer
      Aggregate mode: each returned group's row count, largest first, ties in key order
      with null keys last. At most 100; `omitted` counts the rest. Null in rows mode.
  columns: table of (kind, name, dtype, values)
      Rows mode: the chosen columns, in the order asked, or in dataset order, at most
      10; `omitted` counts the rest. Aggregate mode: the `group_by` keys, one value per
      group.
  measures: table of (kind, column, fn, values)
      Aggregate mode: the counts and statistics asked for, in the order asked. Empty in
      rows mode.
  literal_measures: table of (kind, column, fn, values)
      Aggregate mode: the `min`, `max` and `median` measures asked for, in the order
      asked. Empty in rows mode.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `frame` names no frame Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists up to 5 frame
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `frame` is a Handle of another kind. `allowed` names `frame`.
  unknown_column (3)
      A name in `filter`, `mode.columns`, `mode.order.column`, `mode.group_by` or
      `mode.measures` is not a column of the frame. `candidates` lists close matches;
      `issues` lists every unknown name.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range: a filter, `group_by` or
      `measures` past its caps, a value that does not fit its op, a value whose type
      does not fit its column, or a numeric measure on a column that is not numeric.
      `issues` lists every one.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `frame`. Load it again.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  export-frame: Write the whole frame out as CSV.
  list-handles: Find a frame Handle to read.
  value-summary: Read one column's top values and bounds off a profile.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge query-frame --frame frame_7f3a9c2e --filter '[[{"column":"age","op":"gt","value":40}]]' --mode '{"kind":"rows","columns":["age","city"],"limit":2}'
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e","mode":"rows","total_rows":6,"matched_rows":3,"row_positions":[1,3],"group_count":null,"group_sizes":null,"columns":{"fields":["kind","name","dtype","values"],"rows":[["cells","age","Int64",[41,55]],["cells","city","String",["south","east"]]]},...}
  $ dataforge query-frame --frame frame_7f3a9c2e --mode '{"kind":"aggregate","group_by":["city"],"measures":[{"column":"income","fn":"mean"}]}'
  {...,"mode":"aggregate","total_rows":6,"matched_rows":6,"row_positions":null,"group_count":4,"group_sizes":[2,2,1,1],"columns":{"fields":["kind","name","dtype","values"],"rows":[["cells","city","String",["north","south","east",null]]]},"measures":{"fields":["kind","column","fn","values"],"rows":[["measure","income","mean",[52000.5,63500.375,73000.25,48000.0]]]},...}
commands.resolve-recipe:
usage: dataforge resolve-recipe --routing <string> [--hyperparameters <json>] [--estimates <json>]

Resolve a routing into a recipe Handle that lists the units to fit.

Use when:
  Call this after `route` to get the work `fit_unit` does. The recipe fixes every unit's
  hyperparameters and every column's estimates from the profile the routing was made
  from, once, so each unit fits the same way every time. It reads the routing's own
  dials, so a dial you set on `route` holds here too. The result lists the units by
  value: the joint `mice` and `knn` blocks, and one unit per other column that fills
  values. Columns routed to `passthrough` or `dropped`, and indicator columns, train
  nothing and have no unit. Each unit shows the hyperparameters it trains with. To tune
  a unit, pass `hyperparameters`: the fields you set replace the resolved ones, and the
  rest stay. Estimates are facts the recipe reads off the profile for some columns: the
  two mode centres and centroid features of a bimodal column, and the range a
  `bounded_discrete` column's predictions snap into. The result shows them; pass
  `estimates` to replace one, field by field, as with `hyperparameters`. A forced
  bimodal column the profile found one mode in has no centres, and fits only once you
  set both. `feature_cols` replaces the whole list. To change a recipe, call
  `resolve_recipe` again with every override you want; that makes a new recipe Handle
  and leaves the old one as it was.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --routing <string>, required
      A routing Handle, such as `routing_7f3a9c2e`.
  --hyperparameters <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Hyperparameters you set, one entry per unit.
      Fields: dataforge schema resolve-recipe hyperparameters
  --estimates <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Estimates you set, one entry per column.
      Fields: dataforge schema resolve-recipe estimates

Returns ResolveRecipeResult, as one JSON object:
  recipe: string
      Recipe Handle, such as `recipe_7f3a9c2e`. It holds its own copy of the routing.
  routing: string
      The routing Handle read.
  profile: string
      The profile Handle the routing was made from.
  units: table of (unit_id, strategy, columns, hyperparameters)
      Every unit, in routing order: a joint block where its first column sits in the
      dataset. Empty when no column fills values. At most 50; past 50, `omitted` counts
      the rest and names `explain_routing`, whose columns give each one's id as
      `<strategy>:<column>`.
  estimates: table of (column, center1, center2, feature_cols, domain_snap_bounds)
      Every column that reads estimates, in routing order. Empty when none does. At most
      15; past 15, `omitted` counts the rest.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `routing` names no routing Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists routing
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `routing` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_unit (3)
      A `hyperparameters` entry names a unit the routing does not have. `candidates`
      lists close matches; `issues` lists every problem entry.
  unknown_column (3)
      An `estimates` entry names a column the routing does not have, as its `column` or
      in `feature_cols`. `candidates` lists close matches.
  duplicate_key (2)
      `hyperparameters` names the same unit twice, or `estimates` the same column.
  estimates_not_applicable (2)
      An `estimates` entry names a column whose strategy reads no estimates, or sets a
      field its strategy does not read.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type, a hyperparameter record holds a key or value it
      does not take, or its `kind` is not the unit's strategy; a `feature_cols` entry is
      the column itself or not numeric; or `domain_snap_bounds` has `low` above `high`.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `routing` or its profile.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find recipe Handles made earlier.
  route: Make the routing Handle to resolve.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"knn"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_9e0f1a2b","routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_5a6b7c8d --hyperparameters '[{"unit_id":"knn","hyperparameters":{"kind":"knn","n_neighbors":10}}]'
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_3c4d5e6f","routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"gmm_sampling"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_2e3f4a5b",...}
  $ dataforge resolve-recipe --routing routing_2e3f4a5b --estimates '[{"column":"income","center1":48000,"center2":66000}]'
  {...,"recipe":"recipe_7a8b9c0d","routing":"routing_2e3f4a5b","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
commands.route:
usage: dataforge route --profile <string> [--strategies <json>] [--default-strategy <default_strategy>] [--model-choice <model_choice>] [--exclude-columns <array>] [--skip-columns <array>] [--thresholds <json>]

Route every column of a profile to an imputation strategy, into a routing Handle.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` to decide how each column's missing values are filled.
  Routing reads only the profile, never the rows. Each column gets a strategy and a
  Routing Reason: the one rule that fixed it. Columns you list in `strategies` take your
  strategy with reason `authored`; every other column is routed from its profile, or
  takes `default_strategy` when you set one. A column you force onto `knn`, `mice`,
  `cluster_conditional` or `gmm_sampling` past the Feasibility Floor still trains, and
  the `forced_past_feasibility` warning names it. Non-numeric columns keep their missing
  values. To change a routing, call `route` again; that makes a new routing Handle and
  leaves the old one as it was.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`.
  --strategies <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Strategies you set, one entry per column.
      Fields: dataforge schema route strategies
  --default-strategy <one of mean|median|mode|knn|mice|mnar|dropped|passthrough|cluster_conditional|gmm_sampling>, optional
      The strategy every unlisted numeric column takes. Unlisted columns that are not
      numeric stay `passthrough`. Null routes every unlisted column from its profile.
  --model-choice <one of bayesian_ridge|random_forest_regressor|gradient_boosting_regressor>, optional
      The estimator the MICE block trains with. Null lets the Estimator Ladder pick it
      from the block's nonlinearity. Setting it with no `mice` column fails.
  --exclude-columns <list of string>, optional
      Columns to leave out of this and every later phase, added to what the profile
      already excludes. Null means none.
  --skip-columns <list of string>, optional
      Columns routing leaves as they are: `passthrough` with reason `soft_excluded`, and
      never a predictor. Null means none.
  --thresholds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Dials, grouped by what they judge, each with its default and range.
      Fields: dataforge schema route thresholds

Returns RouteResult, as one JSON object:
  routing: string
      Routing Handle, such as `routing_7f3a9c2e`. It stores every column's Routing
      Evidence.
  profile: string
      The profile Handle that was routed.
  mice_estimator: one of bayesian_ridge|random_forest_regressor|gradient_boosting_regressor
      The estimator the MICE block trains with; null when no column takes `mice`.
  estimator_reason: object
      Why `mice_estimator` was chosen; null when it is null.
  census: table of (strategy, count)
      Columns per strategy, over every column, most first.
  columns: table of (column, semantic_type, strategy, reason)
      Every column but the excluded ones: those that fill or drop values first, then
      `passthrough`, each group in dataset order. At most 100; past 100, `omitted`
      counts the rest and names `explain_routing`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` names no profile Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists profile
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      An argument names a column the profile's frame lacks. `candidates` lists close
      matches; `issues` lists every problem argument.
  duplicate_key (2)
      `strategies` names the same column twice.
  declaration_conflict (4)
      Two declarations contradict: a listed or grouping column that is excluded or
      skipped, or an excluded target.
  strategy_not_declarable (2)
      A column that is not numeric, or that profiling skipped, is given a strategy other
      than `passthrough` or `dropped`.
  constant_fill_missing (2)
      A `constant` entry has no `constant_fill`.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range, or an entry sets
      `constant_fill` or `grouping_variable` its strategy does not read.
  invalid_dial_value (2)
      `signal_score_middle_tier_min` is above `signal_score_top_tier_min`.
  no_mice_block (5)
      `model_choice` is set but no column takes `mice`.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  list-handles: Find routing Handles made earlier.
  profile: Make the profile Handle to route.

Cost: reads only stored records; it does not grow with the data.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge route --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --strategies '[{"column":"income","strategy":"median"}]'
  {...,"routing":"routing_5a6b7c8d","profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
commands.split:
usage: dataforge split --profile <string> [--scheme <json>] [--seed <integer>] [--thresholds <json>]

Split the frame behind a profile into a test frame and folds, each a new frame Handle.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` to make train, validation and test frames. Every scheme
  returns one shape: an optional `test` frame and a list of `folds`, each with a `train`
  and an optional `validation` frame, so a train/test split is one fold with no
  validation and holdout-CV is a `test` plus `k` folds. Each new frame keeps the
  profile's declarations (targets, types, sentinels, exclusions), so a later `profile`
  of a fold may add to them but not contradict them. The profile-stratified schemes
  balance every signal the profile flags, not only the target; `fallbacks` reports each
  step a threshold forced, with the dial to turn. The source frame is never changed.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`. Its frame is split.
  --scheme <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      How to split, chosen by `kind`; null means `profile_stratified` with its defaults.
      Fields: dataforge schema split scheme
  --seed <integer>, optional
      Seed of every shuffle. Null means a fixed default, so the same call gives the same
      split. Constraints: at least 0; at most 4294967295.
  --thresholds <JSON, inline or @file.json>, optional
      Dials of the profile-stratified schemes, each with its default and range.
      Fields: dataforge schema split thresholds

Returns SplitPartitions, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      The profile Handle that was split.
  frame: string
      The frame Handle the profile was made from, whose rows were split.
  scheme: one of random|time|group|kfold|group_kfold|repeated_kfold|holdout_cv|profile_stratified|profile_stratified_kfold
      The scheme used.
  seed: integer
      The seed used: yours, or the fixed default when you passed null.
  stratified_on: string
      The target the split balanced; null when it balanced none.
  test: string
      Frame Handle of the held-out rows; null for the k-fold schemes, which hold none
      out.
  test_rows: integer
      Rows in `test`; null when it is null.
  folds: table of (index, repeat, train, validation, train_rows, validation_rows)
      Every fold, in repeat then index order. At most 100.
  stratification: object
      Signal counts for the profile-stratified schemes; null for the others.
  fallbacks: table of (fallback, count, dials)
      Every fallback taken, each with the dials behind it. Empty when none.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).

Errors (Error Code, exit code):
  unknown_handle (3)
      `profile` names no profile Handle in this Workspace. `candidates` lists profile
      Handles, newest first.
  wrong_handle_kind (2)
      `profile` is a Handle of another kind.
  unknown_column (3)
      `time_column`, `group_column` or `target` names no column of the frame.
      `candidates` lists close matches.
  declaration_conflict (4)
      `time_column` or `group_column` is excluded.
  stratify_without_target (2)
      `stratify` is true but the profile declares no target.
  stratify_on_continuous_target (5)
      The target has too few rows per value to stratify on, as a continuous target does.
      The profile-stratified schemes bin it instead.
  invalid_argument (2)
      An argument has the wrong type or is out of its range; `target` is not a declared
      target, or is unset when several are declared; `k` is above the rows or groups; `k
      * repeats` is above 100; both `test_size` and `cutoff` are set; or `cutoff` does
      not match `time_column`.
  incompatible_artifact (6)
      Another library format version wrote `profile`.
  invalid_setting (2)
      A Workspace Setting is invalid. The message names it and its source.

See Also:
  export-frame: Write a fold's frame to CSV.
  list-handles: Find frame Handles made earlier.
  profile: Make the profile Handle to split, or profile a fold.

Cost: grows with the data. On large data, run it in the background or with a longer
timeout.

Example:
  $ dataforge load --path train.csv
  {...,"frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e",...}
  $ dataforge profile --frame frame_7f3a9c2e
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e",...}
  $ dataforge split --profile profile_1b2c3d4e --scheme '{"kind":"kfold","k":3}'
  {...,"profile":"profile_1b2c3d4e","frame":"frame_7f3a9c2e","scheme":"kfold","seed":42,"stratified_on":null,"test":null,...}
commands.top-associations:
usage: dataforge top-associations --profile <string> [--column <string>] [--metric <metric>] [--min-strength <number>] [--offset <integer>] [--limit <integer>]

List the most strongly associated column pairs off a profile Handle, strongest first.

Use when:
  Call this after `profile` to find columns that go together: near-duplicates to drop,
  predictors for imputation, or the features most related to a target. Pearson (two
  numeric columns), Cramér's V (two categorical columns) and η² (a numeric and a
  categorical column) come in one list sorted by strength, the absolute value of the
  measure. Set `column` to a target to rank features against it. Pairs whose measure
  could not be computed are left out. It reads the stored profile only, so it is cheap
  and never recomputes. The same arguments always return the same page.

Flags (a flag left out is null, which means its default):
  --profile <string>, required
      A profile Handle, such as `profile_7f3a9c2e`.
  --column <string>, optional
      Only pairs that include this column, which is then always `column_a`. Null means
      every pair.
  --metric <one of pearson|cramers_v|eta_squared>, optional
      Only this metric: `pearson`, `cramers_v` or `eta_squared`. Null means all three.
  --min-strength <number>, optional
      Only pairs at least this strong, from 0 to 1. Null means no floor. Constraints: at
      least 0; at most 1.
  --offset <integer>, optional
      How many matching pairs to skip, for the next page. Null means 0. Constraints: at
      least 0.
  --limit <integer>, optional
      Most pairs to return, from 1 to 100. Null means 100. Constraints: at least 1; at
      most 100.

Returns TopAssociationsResult, as one JSON object:
  profile: string
      The profile Handle read.
  total: integer
      How many pairs match the filters.
  offset: integer
      How many matching pairs this page skipped.
  pairs: table of (column_a, column_b, metric, value, near_redundant)
      Matching pairs by strength, strongest first; ties by metric (`pearson`,
      `cramers_v`, `eta_squared`), then dataset order. At most 100; when more remain,
      `omitted` counts them and names `top_associations`.
  near_redundant_dials: table of (metric, dial)
      For each metric, the dial behind `near_redundant`.
  Every result also has `warnings` (caveats; read them first) and `omitted` (cut lists,
  each naming the command that returns the rest).
